title: Backyard Astronomer Films Colossal 'Godzilla' Plasma Cloud on the Sun
summary: Imagine looking at the sun and seeing a monster. Not a real one, but a colossal cloud of glowing plasma that looks like Godzilla looming over the solar surface. That's exactly what astrophotographer Mark Johnston captured from his backyard in Scottsdale, Arizona. His remarkable footage, taken on May 31, 2026, reveals a solar prominence—a massive structure of superheated plasma suspended above the sun by magnetic fields. Johnston also filmed another prominence on May 22, showing streams of material cascading back toward the sun as coronal rain. These aren't flames; there's no fire on the sun. Johnston explains that the hydrogen on the sun is so hot it glows, much like a stove burner glowing red-hot without actual flames. The motion you see isn't wind either. It's primarily controlled by magnetic fields, with gravity playing a lesser role. 'The hydrogen on the limb is ionized, so magnetic fields pull it along invisible field lines,' Johnston told Space.com. He used a 160mm refractor telescope equipped with a specialized hydrogen-alpha solar filter, which isolates a specific wavelength of light to reveal the sun's dynamic atmosphere. Solar prominences are immense, often stretching many times the size of Earth. When viewed against the dark backdrop of space, they appear as glowing arches or curtains. Against the sun's bright face, they're called filaments and look like dark ribbons because they're cooler and denser than the surrounding material. Johnston's dedication is clear: 'I try to image the Sun every clear morning, and I'm always looking for interesting features.' His work underscores that with the right equipment and safety precautions—never look directly at the sun without certified solar filters—amazing celestial phenomena are accessible to amateur astronomers. He has even authored 'The Solar Observer's Handbook' to guide others. So next time you look up, remember: the sun is not a quiet ball of light; it's a dynamic, magnetic star with surprises waiting to be captured.
why_it_matters: Understanding the Sun's magnetic behavior is crucial for predicting space weather, which can disrupt satellites, power grids, and communications; amateur images like these help scientists track solar activity and also show that anyone with passion can contribute to science.

background_read: Solar prominences have been observed for centuries, first recorded during total solar eclipses when the Moon blocked the bright disk. They are anchored to the Sun's photosphere and can extend hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space — often larger than the entire Earth. The Sun's magnetic field, generated by churning plasma deep inside, goes through an 11-year cycle of activity; during solar maximum, prominences and other phenomena become more frequent. Amateur astronomers like Mark Johnston (from Scottsdale, Arizona — a city near Phoenix) contribute valuable observations using specialized equipment like hydrogen-alpha filters, which reveal the Sun's chromosphere. His book, 'The Solar Observer's Handbook', helps others get started safely. NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory and other space missions also monitor the Sun continuously, confirming that it is a dynamic, ever-changing star.

perspectives.description: Johnston's work demonstrates that amateur astronomers can capture stunning, scientifically valuable images from their own backyards. It makes the Sun's hidden activity accessible, inspiring young people to pursue astronomy and showing that cutting-edge observation doesn't require a professional observatory.

Solar observation carries serious risks — looking at the Sun improperly can cause permanent eye damage. While the article emphasizes safety, many beginners might underestimate the danger or use uncertified filters. Additionally, powerful solar storms associated with increased magnetic activity can threaten modern technology.

The Sun's magnetic field follows an 11-year cycle, with periods of high activity (solar maximum) producing more prominences and flares. This footage was captured in 2026, likely near a solar maximum, offering a natural example of the cycle's peak. Amateur observations complement satellite data to build a fuller picture of solar dynamics.

As the next solar maximum approaches, interest in solar astronomy will grow. More affordable hydrogen-alpha technology could let classrooms and families observe the Sun safely. Integrating such images into school curricula could spark a new generation of scientists focused on the Sun-Earth connection and space weather preparedness.
